# Common-normal allocation hulls of ordinary depth regions

This note gives a rigorous inner region for the middle mixed-depth region
of three actual fibers. It is strictly stronger pointwise than separately
adding ordinary middle depth and optimized endpoint depth. An exact
compatible simplex example nevertheless makes the proposed region empty
at the OC target. Universal nonemptiness of this construction is therefore
false, even before replacing ordinary depth regions by elementary cores.

## 1. Definitions

Let d>=1 and let A,K,B be full-dimensional compact convex bodies in R^d,
with (A+B)/2 contained in K. Put the three bodies at integer bases -1,0,1
and use the sum of their ordinary d-volume measures. Let Delta(y) be the
raw mixed halfspace depth at (0,y), y in K, over every closed ambient
halfspace containing that point.

For a body F define its ordinary raw depth function f_F on F and its
ordinary depth regions

    D_F(p)={x in F:f_F(x)>=p}, p>0;     D_F(0)=F.

These are compact convex sets, possibly empty. To see closedness, cap
volume through x depends jointly continuously on x and on a unit normal:
away from the limiting hyperplane the indicators converge, and that
hyperplane has zero d-volume. Minimization over the compact unit sphere
preserves continuity. Convexity follows because a halfspace containing a
convex combination contains at least one of the combined points. We use
empty+F=empty and conv(empty)=empty.

For r>=0 define

    C_r = intersection_{p_A,p_K,p_B>=0, p_A+p_K+p_B=r}
            conv( D_K(p_K) union
                     ((D_A(p_A)+D_B(p_B))/2) ).          (1)

Every set in this intersection is compact and convex, or empty. Moreover
C_r is contained in K: use the allocation (0,r,0) and the actual inclusion
(A+B)/2 subset K. Thus each nonempty C_r is a compact convex set of actual
middle-fiber candidate points. The family is decreasing in r. Indeed,
for an allocation summing to r one can increase its entries to sum to
r'>r; all three depth regions, and hence its allocation hull, only shrink.
Membership in C_{r'} therefore implies membership in each hull at level r.

## 2. The common-normal inclusion

**Theorem.** For every r>=0,

    C_r subset {y in K:Delta(y)>=r}.                     (2)

**Proof.** Suppose y in C_r and an actual closed ambient halfspace H
containing (0,y) has captured volumes U,q,V with U+q+V<r. Choose
p_A>U, p_K>q, p_B>V with p_A+p_K+p_B=r; for example add one third of the
positive deficit to each captured volume.

First assume H has a nonzero continuous normal. Translate its boundary
parallel toward (0,y), decreasing its cap, until it goes through (0,y).
The new cap volumes remain strictly below the chosen allocations. Write
its continuous thresholds at the three fibers as h_A,h_K,h_B; they obey
h_K=(h_A+h_B)/2 and h_K=u.y for one common nonzero normal u.

Every point of D_A(p_A) lies strictly below the A cutting plane. Otherwise
that plane is an ordinary halfspace containing a point of own depth at
least p_A while cutting volume less than p_A, a contradiction. The same
holds for K and B. It follows that their endpoint midpoint set lies
strictly below the middle cutting plane, as does D_K(p_K). Empty depth
regions cause no difficulty. Nonempty regions are compact, so their convex
hull also lies strictly below that plane. It cannot contain y, contradicting
membership in the allocation hull in (1).

For a purely integer-coordinate halfspace, its middle trace contains all
of K, and at least one endpoint trace contains its whole endpoint body.
The strict allocations therefore have p_K>|K| and p_A>|A| or p_B>|B|.
Thus D_K(p_K) is empty and the endpoint Minkowski sum is empty. Its
allocation hull is empty, again a contradiction. This proves (2) for all
closed ambient halfspaces, including supporting and full/empty cuts.
QED.

The convex hull is essential to retaining the common continuous normal:
both of its pieces lie on the SAME forbidden side in the contradiction.
There is no interchange of independent directional infima in this proof.

## 3. Relation to simpler midpoint certificates

For 0<s<=min(|A|,|B|) put

    R_s=intersection_{0<=p<=s}
                     (D_A(p)+D_B(s-p))/2.               (3)

Exactly the endpoint portion of the preceding proof gives endpoint-only
raw depth at least s at every point of R_s. A deficient endpoint cap with
masses U+V<s permits an allocation p>U, s-p>V, and both depth regions would
lie strictly below the same source plane. Pure integer caps contain a
whole endpoint and have mass at least min(|A|,|B|)>=s.

Consequently D_K(t) intersect R_s is a valid mixed-depth certificate at
level t+s. It is also contained in C_{t+s}. For any allocation in (1), if
p_K<=t, its K region already contains the point. If p_K>t, then
p_A+p_B<s. Increase p_A,p_B to nonnegative p_A',p_B' summing to s.
Membership in R_s puts the point in their smaller midpoint depth-region
sum, and hence in the original allocation's midpoint sum.

The region R_s contains (D_A(s)+D_B(s))/2 by nesting. More generally,
D_K(t) intersect (D_A(p)+D_B(q))/2 is contained in C_{t+min(p,q)}.
This follows by the same allocation dichotomy. Thus C_r includes the
ordinary middle-depth plus midpoint-capacity certificates, including
those obtained from the archived additive-midpoint certificate. This
statement does not assert that it contains EVERY superlevel set of the
exact separated quantity f_K+P, since (3) is only an inner region for
the true endpoint-only depth.

## 4. Strict pointwise gain: complete interval calculation

Take d=1, A=B=[0,1], K=[0,2], and r=4/3. Then

    C_(4/3)={5/6}.                                     (4)

For a length-one endpoint, D_A(p)=D_B(p)=[p,1-p] for
0<=p<=1/2 and is empty for p>1/2. For the middle,
D_K(t)=[t,2-t] for 0<=t<=1 and is empty for t>1.

We first show 5/6 lies in every allocation hull. If an endpoint level
exceeds 1/2, its midpoint sum is empty, but then t<5/6; the nonempty
middle interval [t,2-t] contains 5/6. If t>1, then the endpoint levels
sum to 4/3-t<1/3, so both are below 1/2. Their midpoint interval is
[(4/3-t)/2,1-(4/3-t)/2], which contains 5/6. If neither of these cases
holds, all regions are nonempty. The middle interval has upper endpoint
2-t>=1, and the endpoint midpoint interval has lower endpoint at most
1/2. Their convex hull therefore contains 5/6. This covers all
allocations, including equality in the level bounds.

For the reverse inclusion, use allocations

    p_A=1/2+epsilon, p_B=0, t=5/6-epsilon,

for arbitrarily small epsilon>0. Their hulls are just D_K(t), so membership
in their intersection forces y>=5/6. Next take

    t=1+epsilon, p_A=1/3-epsilon, p_B=0.

Their hulls are just the endpoint midpoint intervals, forcing y<=5/6 as
epsilon decreases to zero. This proves (4), with the limiting argument
involving only inequalities for one fixed candidate y.

At y=5/6, ordinary middle depth is 5/6 and exact endpoint-only depth is
1/3. Their separated sum is therefore 7/6, strictly below the new
certificate 4/3. The actual mixed depth is 3/2. Indeed, for endpoint
intervals [0,1] and h in [0,1], their optimized upper-tail sum is
min(2(1-h),1), and their optimized lower-tail sum is min(2h,1). If both
cuts are proper their tail sum is fixed by the threshold sum; if one is
empty the other's tail gives the same lower bound, and if one is full
the sum is at least one. Balanced thresholds or a finite saturated tilt
attain the stated minima. At y=5/6, the full upper and lower costs are
respectively 7/6+1/3=3/2 and 5/6+1=11/6. Pure integer caps have mass three.
Thus the common-normal inclusion yields a genuine strict pointwise gain
while correctly remaining a lower certificate.

As an exact sharpness calibration, if A=K=B=[0,1] and 0<r<=1/2,
every allocation region is nonempty, and direct interval convex hulls give

    C_r=[r/3,1-r/3].

Indeed their left endpoints are min(t,(r-t)/2), whose maximum is r/3.
This is the actual mixed-depth region, since the mixed depth is
3 min(y,1-y). Thus the level r in (2) cannot be universally increased.

## 5. An explicit ordinary inner-core variant

For any body F with volume V_F and centroid g_F, define

    E_F(p)=g_F+[1-(p/(Gamma_d V_F))^(1/d)](F-g_F)
                                      for 0<=p<=Gamma_d V_F,
    E_F(p)=empty                      for p>Gamma_d V_F.

The archived ordinary depth-root concavity and ordinary Gruenbaum imply
E_F(p) subset D_F(p). Equivalently, one can scale a centroid half-cap of F
about any endpoint w in F to obtain the same capacity lower bound.
Substituting E for D in (1) gives a universally explicit smaller inner
region and hence preserves (2). It does not establish its nonemptiness.

## 6. Exact two-allocation emptiness at the OC target

This obstruction applies BOTH to the full field C_r and to its explicit
inner-core variant. Let

    T={(x1,x2):x1>=0,x2>=0,x1+x2<=1},   V=|T|=1/2,
    A=(1/10)T, K=B=T,   Gamma=4/9.

Their lifted convex hull is an actual full-dimensional convex body with
exactly these three integer fibers: their endpoint midpoint is
D=(11/20)T subset T. The total volume is M=(201/100)V, so the OC target is

    r=Gamma M/2=Gamma(201/200)V.

A triangle of area W has maximum ordinary raw depth Gamma W. Ordinary
Gruenbaum proves the lower value at the centroid; conversely some
barycentric coordinate of any point is at least 1/3, and the cap toward
that vertex has relative area at most (2/3)^2=Gamma.

Use first the allocation (p_A,p_K,p_B)=(0,r,0). Since r>Gamma V,
D_K(r) is empty. Its hull is exactly D, forcing C_r subset D.

Use second the allocation

    p_A=2Gamma V/100,
    p_K=Gamma(197/200)V=197V/450,
    p_B=0.

These sum to r. The A level exceeds its maximal own depth Gamma V/100,
so the endpoint midpoint sum is empty. Its hull is only D_K(197V/450).
But every x in D satisfies x1+x2<=11/20. The middle halfspace
{x1+x2<=x1(point)+x2(point)} contains x and has area at most
(11/20)^2 V=121V/400. Since

    121/400 < 197/450,

D is disjoint from D_K(197V/450). These TWO allocations already make
C_r empty. The inner-core variant is a subset and is empty as well.

For the explicit core one can also see separation directly: its second
K core has scale 1-sqrt(197/200) about the triangle centroid. Its minimum
coordinate sum is (2/3)sqrt(197/200)>11/20, as verified by squaring positive
numbers. No infinite-family or numerical nonemptiness argument is used.

Thus universal nonemptiness of either allocation construction is FALSE.
This is not an OC counterexample; the actual source is the archived safe
tiny-endpoint family. The obstruction locates information lost by replacing
all directional quantiles with ordinary depth regions. Neither root
concavity nor optimizing scalar allocations repairs this lost information.

For the volume window (1/4,1,121/100) discussed in the coverage audit,
the middle own-depth level Gamma=4/9 would require endpoint payment
23/225 to reach the target41/75. Formula (3) supplies a precise sufficient
intersection D_K(4/9) intersect R_(23/225), but this note does NOT prove
that intersection is always nonempty. All its endpoint depth levels are
below their respective ordinary centroid guarantees; that fact alone
does not align this region with the middle ordinary depth region.
